newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-France may hit EMU deficit goal - Strauss-Kahn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France may hit EMU deficit goal - Strauss-Kahn.

text.p: French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, in remarks likely to delight Germany, was quoted on Wednesday saying Paris may meet or even undershoot borrowing targets for Europe's single currency this year.

Strauss-Kahn, speaking to German weekly Die Zeit, signalled greater French willingness to try and score a direct hit on the Maastricht treaty budget deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.
He also said he expected Portugal, Italy and Spain to join the first wave of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"Thanks to accelerated economic growth we could come very close to three percent -- perhaps even below it," Strauss-Kahn told Die Zeit in an interview released ahead of publication on Thursday.
"So when the selection of the euro members is made in the spring of 1998 we will be in as good form as our EU partners."
On Monday, Strauss-Kahn unveiled a 32 billion francs ($5.2 billion) package aimed at knocking two-fifths of a percentage point off France's deficit, which has been running at 3.5 to 3.7 percent.

But his comments then left open whether France would end up a couple of tenths over the strict "three-point-zero" interpretation of Maastricht demanded by a group of German euro hardliners led by Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber.

Stoiber is widely seen as coveting German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's position as leader of the Bavaria-based Christian Social Union party, leaving Waigel little room to allow France to fudge EMU without endangering his own position.

Waigel gave Strauss-Kahn's deficit-cutting plan a lukewarm welcome on Monday. In remarks on Tuesday apparently directed at France he renewed his commitment to Germany's tough "three-point-zero" line on the deficit.

Strauss-Kahn told Die Zeit that he did not consider the budget deficit to be the most important measure of a country's fitness to join EMU, adding that economic convergence was more important for the viability of the common currency.
He also said France's new Socialist-led government would do all it could to meet EMU targets, but had inherited a bloated budget deficit from the previous conservative government.
"You can be certain that the budget for 1998 will be drafted with a deficit of three percent," he said.

The French Finance Minister also gave weight to the belief that a broad economic and monetary union was likely, which has led financial markets to speculate that the euro would be weaker than the mark at its start in 1999.

This has contributed to a pounding of Europe's anchor currency on financial markets. The dollar hovered just below 1.83 marks in afternoon trade on Wednesday, after earlier hitting fresh 71-month highs.

Strauss-Kahn said he hoped many European countries would qualify to join in the first wave of monetary union when the European Union decides who makes the grade early next year based on economic performance in 1997.

"The Benelux countries will certainly be there," he said. "Portugal, Spain and Italy as well, I think. I am convinced that the euro can become a truly European currency and not just a Franco-German currency. That would be far too narrow."
Strauss-Kahn also supported launching the euro on schedule and alleged that those who called for a delay of monetary union were really working towards derailing the project altogether.

"Whoever considers the euro to be a bad thing shouldn't talk of delay but should put his cards on the table. I, on the other hand, think the euro is a good thing and therefore want to launch it at the agreed time," he said.

Strauss-Kahn added he did not believe a delay to EMU was legally possible, and if it took place would cause turbulence on financial markets. "Europe needs the euro. Otherwise we cannot match the monetary power of the U.S.," he said.
Commenting on the mark's current weakness, Strauss-Kahn rejected the view that the euro would be a weaker currency.
"All indications are that the euro will be a stable currency," he said. "France has had a hard currency for 15 years and Germany too, of course. Why should this change?"
-- douglas.busvine@reuters.com (Bonn 49-228-26097 150) ($ = 6.134 French Francs)
